newsitem.title: UK: Labour's Blair against sale of London Underground.
newsitem.headline: Labour's Blair against sale of London Underground.

text.p: Opposition Labour leader Tony Blair on Tuesday proposed a private/public partnership to increase investment in London Underground as an alternative to the government's plans to privatise the rail network.
Blair said the Conservatives' plans, leaked in Sunday's papers, would offer the prospect of a windfall gain for private shareholders but no new investment until 2001 at the earliest.

"So privatisation would be a poor deal for the taxpayers. It would offer no strategic control over a vital public asset. And it would, yet again, be selling off a monopoly public service with no prospect of competition," he told a conference.
An alternative to privatisation would be to bring in private sector capital and skills to modernise London Underground stations and tap their potential for retail development, Blair said.

"There could be new D.R.O. schemes -- design, renew and operate -- where the private sector would refurbish and maintain tracks and tunnels. Train manufacturers could be contracted to provide trains to meet the service level set and run by London Underground," the Labour leader added.
He said this would provide a better service for Tube users and a better deal for taxpayers.
"And it would mean that we could make a start on improving the underground within months of the election of a new government, rather than doing nothing until the next century.
"It would offer Londoners a new way between the status quo and dogmatic wholesale privatisation," Blair said.

He said Labour's transport spokesman, Andrew Smith, would be writing to LU chairman Peter Ford on Tuesday to outline the party's proposals so the Underground would be in a position to bring forward plans as soon as possible after the election.
